’El. The oldest Semitic term for God is ’el (corresponding to Akkadian ilu(m), Canaanite ’el or ’il, and Arabic ’el as an element in personal names). The etymology of the word is obscure. It is commonly thought that the term derived from a root ’yl or ’wl, meaning ‘‘to be powerful’’ (cf. yesh le-el yadi, ‘‘It is in the power of my hand,’’ Gen. 31:29; cf. Deut. 28:32; Micah 2:1). But the converse may be true; since power is an essential element in the concept of deity, the term for deity may have been used in the transferred sense of ‘‘power.’’ In Akkadian, ilu(m), and plural ilu and ilanu, is used in reference to any individual god as well as to divine beings in general; but it is not employed as the personal name of any god. In Ugaritic Canaanite, however, il occurs much more frequently as the personal name of the highest god el than as the common noun ‘‘god’’ (pl., ilm; fem., ilt). In the Ugaritic myths El is the head of the Canaanite pantheon, the ancestor of the other gods and goddesses, and the creator of the earth and its creatures; but he generally fades into the background and plays a minor role in the preserved myths.
